images.photo: <head>Welcome to the AVRI Photo Gallery</head><body>AVRI's Kim and Tracy working on a 16ft Indian Rock python, Python molurus</body>

Venomous snakebite is a major
Public Health issue in Sri Lanka
<head>The Hump-nosed Viper, Hypnale hypnale</head><<body>is responsible for the most bites</body>
<head>An endemic species</head><body>No antivenom has ever been created to neutralize its venom</body>
<head>Venomous snakebite plagues those living mostly in rural areas</head><body>People often unable to reach or afford medical help</body>
<head>The Russell's Viper, Daboia russelii</head><body>with fangs exposed</body>
<head>The Russell's Viper is responsible for the most deaths in Sri Lanka</head><body>Due to venomous snakebite</body>

Agricultural workers are often bitten
Death or disability may mean the loss of a family's primary wage earner
<head>In Sri Lanka</head><body>The venom of the Russell's viper has properties that do not occur in the species on mainland Asia</body>
DonateNOWto help AVRIdevelop a regional specific antivenom for Sri Lanka
<head>The Spectacled Cobra, Naja naja</head><body>causes many deaths in Sri Lanka</body>

The cobra is an important part of religious culture
symbolic representations of the cobra can be found throughout the country
<head>The 'spectacles'</head><<body>on the back of the cobra's hood</body>
<head>A painting inside</head><body>the Buddhist Temple of the Tooth, Sri Dalada Maligawa</body>
<head>AVRI's Roy</head><body>with a large Spectacled cobra</body>
<head>An adult Common Krait</head><body>Bungarus caeruleus</body>
<head>Traditional wattle-and-daub houses are easy for kraits to enter</head><body>People are often bitten at night while sleeping on the floor</body>
<head>A juvenile krait eating a lizard</head><body>the white banding will mostly disappear with age</body>
<head>The Ceylon Krait, Bungarus ceylonicus</head><body>a poorly known endemic species in Sri Lanka</body>
